results.message: What did Augustine mean by "love, and do what you will"?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
The root of the deed decides what the deed is. Augustine wrote: “A father beats a boy, and a slave-dealer caresses him. Name the two things, blows and caresses: who would not choose the caresses and refuse the blows? Look at the persons: it is love that beats, and wickedness that caresses. See what we are pressing on you. People’s deeds are told apart only by the root of love. For many things may be done that look good, and yet do not come from the root of love. Thorns have flowers too. Some actions seem rough, even savage. Yet they are done to train and correct, at love’s bidding. So once and for all, you are given a short rule: Love, and do what you will. If you keep silent, keep silent from love. If you cry out, cry out from love. If you correct, correct from love. If you spare, spare from love. Let the root of love be within you. From this root nothing can grow but what is good.”

A father's blow and a slave-dealer's caress are not the same act, though one is harsh and the other seems kind. The father strikes from love; the dealer flatters to harm. So let love be the root, Augustine says, and whatever grows from that root will be right. This is not permission to do as you please and call it love afterward. It is a warning that the same outward deed, done from different roots, becomes a different thing entirely. The words come from a homily on the First Epistle of John, one of the tractates Augustine gave as teaching.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo
